mainTopic: The exemptions of an אונן and of one guarding the dead, and showing respect for the dead
overview: The amud opens in the middle of a ברייתא about an אונן, a person whose dead relative is not yet buried. On weekdays he is exempt from blessings, זימון, קריאת שמע, תפילה, תפילין and all מצוות. On שבת he acts normally. רבי יוחנן explains that the תנא קמא and רבן שמעון בן גמליאל differ about תשמיש המטה. The גמרא then sets the ברייתא against the משנה's words 'lying before him'. רב פפא limits the ברייתא to that case, and רב אשי says that as long as burial is his duty, the dead counts as before him. Next the גמרא learns that a relative is exempt even when he is not guarding the body, and a guard is exempt even when the dead is not his relative. Someone walking in a בית הקברות is limited only within four אמות of a grave. The ברייתא about guards adds rules for two guards and for a boat, and רבינא explains that the dispute is about worrying over mice. The amud closes with respect for the dead: not riding on bones or a ספר תורה except in danger, the duty and reward of escorting a מת, and the story of רבי חייא and רבי יונתן in the cemetery. That story's proof from בניהו בן יהוידע continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Weekday exemptions of the mourner before burial
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues: on weekdays, others do not bless for the אונן or count him for זימון, and he is exempt from קריאת שמע, תפילה, תפילין and all מצוות.
steps.simpleTranslation: Others do not say a blessing for him, and they do not count him in a זימון. He is exempt from קריאת שמע, from תפילה, from תפילין, and from all the מצוות in the תורה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is still quoting a ברייתא that began on the previous עמוד, listing what a mourner with an unburied relative may not do or does not have to do on a weekday.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier in the ברייתא we learned that he eats in a different room and does not bless for himself. Now it adds that others cannot bless for him or include him in a זימון. He is also freed from every positive מצוה. רב אשי (step 8) connects the exemption to the fact that burial is still his responsibility.

keyTerms.meaning: others say a blessing on his behalf
others include him in the זימון (the group invitation before בִּרְכַּת הַמָּזוֹן)
the מצוות stated in the תורה

steps.confusionAlert: This is not the beginning of the ברייתא. The case (מִי שֶׁמֵּתוֹ מוּטָּל לְפָנָיו, eating in another room) was set up on the previous עמוד.

phrases.english: And others do not recite a blessing on his behalf,
and others do not include him in a zimun,
and he is exempt from reciting Shema
and from prayer and from tefillin
and from all the מצוות stated in the Torah.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאֵין מְבָרְכִין עָלָיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ברייתא quoted at the end of the previous עמוד.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: On a weekday the אונן is not counted for blessings or זימון and is exempt from all מצוות.

steps.title: On שבת the mourner acts normally
steps.stepSummary: On שבת the אונן reclines, eats meat, drinks wine, blesses, leads and joins a זימון, and is obligated in all מצוות.
steps.simpleTranslation: On שבת he reclines at the meal, eats meat and drinks wine. He blesses and leads a זימון, others bless for him and count him for a זימון, and he is obligated in all the מצוות of the תורה.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא turns to שבת and says the mourner goes back to full normal behavior and full obligation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: On שבת he cannot do anything about the burial, so the reason for exempting him is gone. Also, public mourning is not done on שבת. So every weekday exemption from step 1 is reversed.

keyTerms.meaning: reclines at the meal, the normal way of eating

phrases.english: But on Shabbat he reclines and eats meat
and drinks wine, and recites blessings and leads a zimun,
and others bless on his behalf and include him in a zimun,
and he is obligated in all the מצוות stated in the Torah.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּבְשַׁבָּת מֵיסֵב וְאוֹכֵל בָּשָׂר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the שבת rule, which is the opposite of the weekday rule.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: On שבת the אונן behaves normally and is obligated in all מצוות.

steps.title: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל: obligated in these, obligated in all
steps.stepSummary: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says that since he is obligated in these שבת meal practices, he is obligated in everything.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says: since he became obligated in these, he became obligated in all of them.
steps.whatsHappening: A second תנא, רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, gives his own statement about the mourner on שבת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His words sound just like the end of the תנא קמא's statement, which already said he is obligated in all מצוות. That makes us wonder what he is adding. The next step asks exactly that.

phrases.english: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:
Since he became obligated in these —
phrases.notes: "These" are the שבת meal practices just listed: reclining, meat, wine, blessings and זימון.

phrases.english: he became obligated in all of them.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל אוֹמֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second opinion that seems to repeat the תנא קמא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Being obligated in the שבת practices makes him obligated in all מצוות.

steps.title: What is the difference between the two opinions?
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן asks what the practical difference is between the תנא קמא and רבן שמעון בן גמליאל.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יוחנן said: what is the difference between them?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן notices that both opinions seem to say the same thing, so he asks where they actually differ. He is setting up his own answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both opinions say the mourner is obligated in everything on שבת. If two תנאים are recorded as separate opinions, there must be a case where they rule differently. The question is looking for that case.

keyTerms.meaning: what is the difference between them?

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yochanan said:
What is the difference between them?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי בֵּינַיְיהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks why רבן שמעון בן גמליאל's statement is needed if it seems to match the תנא קמא.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The practical case where the תנא קמא and רבן שמעון בן גמליאל disagree.

steps.title: The difference is marital relations
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן answers that they disagree about תשמיש המטה on שבת.
steps.simpleTranslation: תשמיש המטה (marital relations) is the difference between them.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן answers his own question: the two opinions differ about whether the mourner has marital relations on שבת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תנא קמא holds he is obligated in all מצוות but still refrains from relations, since that is private and does not show mourning in public. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל's 'obligated in all of them' includes even this. So 'all' means something wider for him.

keyTerms.meaning: there is between them, meaning this is their point of difference

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that two statements that sound identical can still hide a real practical disagreement.

phrases.english: Marital relations is the difference between them.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּשְׁמִישׁ הַמִּטָּה אִיכָּא בֵּינַיְיהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 4.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The opinions differ about תשמיש המטה on שבת: the תנא קמא forbids it, and רבן שמעון בן גמליאל obligates it.

steps.title: The ברייתא exempts him even in another room
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges: the ברייתא exempts him from all מצוות even when he is in another room, while the משנה exempts only one whose dead lies before him.
steps.simpleTranslation: In any case, the ברייתא teaches that he is exempt from קריאת שמע, from תפילה, from תפילין, and from all the מצוות in the תורה!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא returns to the weekday part of the ברייתא and uses it to challenge the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says only someone whose dead lies 'before him' is exempt. But the ברייתא talks about a man eating in a different room, and still exempts him from everything. This looks like the ברייתא gives a wider exemption than the משנה.

keyTerms.meaning: in any case, it teaches; used to pull out one point from a source and set aside the rest

steps.confusionAlert: 'In any case' means: set aside the שבת argument we just discussed. The challenge comes from the weekday part of the ברייתא (step 1).

phrases.english: In any case, it teaches:
phrases.notes: The גמרא is going back to the weekday part of the ברייתא, setting aside the שבת argument.

phrases.english: he is exempt from reciting Shema
and from prayer and from tefillin
and from all the מצוות stated in the Torah!

steps.triggerLanguage: קָתָנֵי מִיהַת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the weekday ruling and sets it against the משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's limit that only one whose dead lies before him is exempt.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא exempts him even when he eats in another room, so the exemption seems to go beyond 'lying before him'.

steps.title: רב פפא: the ברייתא means when he turns his face and eats
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא limits the ברייתא's exemption to the case where he has no other room and eats near the body, turning his face away.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: explain the exemption as referring to the case of one who turns his face away and eats.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא answers the challenge by saying the ברייתא's exemption belongs only to one specific case within it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier the ברייתא said that if he has no other room, he turns his face away and eats. רב פפא says the exemption from מצוות goes only with that case, where the body really is in front of him. So the ברייתא matches the משנה's literal 'before him'.

keyTerms.meaning: explain it as / apply it to

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:
Explain it as referring to one who turns his face away and eats.
phrases.notes: This goes back to an earlier line in the ברייתא: if he has no other room, he turns his face away and eats.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּרְגְּמָא אַמַּחֲזִיר פָּנָיו וְאוֹכֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא by narrowing the case of the ברייתא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the source to a specific case
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא exempts him even when he is in another room.
steps.terutzMaskana: The exemption applies only where the body is in front of him and he turns his face to eat.

steps.title: רב אשי: responsibility to bury counts as 'before him'
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי says that as long as burial is his responsibility, it is as if the dead lies before him, and he proves it from פסוקים about אברהם.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: since it is his duty to bury him, it is as if the dead lies before him. As it says, 'And אברהם rose up from before his dead,' and it says, 'that I may bury my dead from before me.' As long as it is his duty to bury him, it is as if he lies before him.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי gives a different answer: the משנה's words 'lying before him' are not meant physically. They mean the burial is still his job.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אברהם was already away from the body, since he 'rose up from before his dead', yet he still calls it 'my dead from before me'. So 'before me' means 'my responsibility'. With that reading, the משנה and the ברייתא agree, and he is exempt even in another room.

keyTerms.meaning: it is placed upon him, meaning it is his duty
it is as if he lies before him

steps.whatToRemember: There are two answers. רב פפא keeps 'before him' literal and limits the ברייתא. רב אשי reads 'before him' as 'his responsibility to bury', so an אונן is exempt even in another room.

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
Since it is placed upon him to bury him,
phrases.notes: There's a wordplay here: 'placed upon him' means his duty, which echoes 'placed before him' in the משנה.

phrases.english: it is as if he lies before him.
As it is stated: "And Abraham rose up from before his dead,"
phrases.notes: בראשית 23:3

phrases.english: and it is stated: "that I may bury my dead from before me."
phrases.notes: בראשית 23:4. He already left the body, but still calls it 'before me'.

phrases.english: As long as it is placed upon him to bury him,
it is as if he lies before him.

steps.triggerLanguage: כֵּיוָן שֶׁמּוּטָּל עָלָיו לְקוֹבְרוֹ, כְּמוּטָל לְפָנָיו דָּמֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second answer to the same קשיא, different from רב פפא's.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining a term in the משנה
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Lying before him' means physically in front of him.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'Lying before him' means burial is still his duty, so he is exempt wherever he is.
steps.whyThisMatters: This answer sets the scope of אנינות: it depends on responsibility for burial, not on where the body is.

steps.title: Only his own dead, not one he is guarding
steps.stepSummary: From the משנה's word 'his dead' the גמרא infers that the exemption is for a relative, not for someone who is just guarding a body.
steps.simpleTranslation: His dead, yes. But one who is guarding the dead, no.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא makes an inference from the משנה's wording: only someone whose own relative died is exempt from מצוות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says 'one whose dead (מֵתוֹ) lies before him'. The word 'his' teaches that the exemption belongs to the person who has the duty of burial. Someone who is only guarding a body does not get this exemption.

keyTerms.meaning: his dead, meaning his own relative
yes ... no; a short way to contrast two cases

phrases.english: His dead, yes,
phrases.notes: This picks up the משנה's word 'his dead': for a relative, yes, he is exempt.

phrases.english: but one who is guarding him, no.

steps.triggerLanguage: מֵתוֹ — אִין, אֲבָל מְשַׁמְּרוֹ — לָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After defining 'lying before him', the גמרא defines 'his dead'.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The exemption applies to a relative whose dead is unburied, not to someone only guarding a body.

steps.title: A ברייתא says even a non-relative who guards the body is exempt
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the inference that only a relative is exempt. A ברייתא exempts anyone guarding a מת, even when it is not his relative.
steps.simpleTranslation: But wasn't it taught in a ברייתא: One who guards a dead body, even if it is not his own dead relative, is exempt from קריאת שמע, from תפילה, from תפילין, and from all the מצוות in the תורה!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that seems to contradict what it just learned from the משנה in step 9.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 9 read 'his dead' to mean only a relative is exempt, and someone who is just guarding the body is not. This ברייתא says plainly that a guard is exempt even when the מת is not his relative. So guarding seems to be a reason for exemption all by itself.

keyTerms.meaning: One who guards or watches over a dead body
His dead, meaning his own relative who died

phrases.english: But wasn't it taught: One who guards the dead,
even though it is not his own dead relative,
is exempt from קריאת שמע and from prayer,
and from תפילין,
and from all the מצוות stated in the תורה!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָתַנְיָא: הַמְשַׁמֵּר אֶת הַמֵּת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the inference of step 9
steps.kashyaTarget: The inference that only a relative is exempt, and a guard is not
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא openly exempts a guard who is not a relative

steps.title: Both a guard and a relative are exempt
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the two sources do not argue. A guard is exempt even if it is not his relative, and a relative is exempt even if he is not guarding.
steps.simpleTranslation: One who guards the body is exempt even if it is not his relative. One whose relative died is exempt even if he is not guarding.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא resolves the challenge by saying that each source teaches a different reason for being exempt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה's 'his dead' does not exclude a guard. It teaches that a relative is exempt even without guarding. The ברייתא adds that guarding alone also exempts. So there are two separate reasons for exemption.
steps.confusionAlert: This answer takes back the conclusion of step 9. In the end, a guard who is not a relative IS exempt.

phrases.aramaic: מְשַׁמְּרוֹ, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵינוֹ מֵתוֹ,
phrases.english: One who guards it, even though it is not his dead relative,
phrases.notes: The גמרא doesn't say 'exempt' here, but that's what it means: both of these people are exempt.

phrases.aramaic: מֵתוֹ אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵינוֹ מְשַׁמְּרוֹ.
phrases.english: and one whose dead relative it is, even though he is not guarding it.

steps.triggerLanguage: מְשַׁמְּרוֹ, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵינוֹ מֵתוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 10
steps.terutzResolutionType: Complementary reading: each source covers a different case
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה's 'his dead' excludes a non-relative guard
steps.terutzMaskana: Both a relative (even if not guarding) and a guard (even if not a relative) are exempt

steps.title: Inference: someone just walking in a cemetery is not exempt
steps.stepSummary: From this answer the גמרא infers that only a relative or a guard is exempt, but someone walking in a בית הקברות is not.
steps.simpleTranslation: His relative, or one guarding: yes, they are exempt. But one who is walking in a cemetery: no, he is not exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws a conclusion from step 11 to set up the next challenge.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the exemption comes from being a relative or from guarding, a person who is simply near the dead, like someone walking through a בית הקברות, would seem to stay obligated in all the מצוות.

phrases.english: His dead relative, or one guarding it: yes, they are exempt,
but one who walks in a cemetery: no, he is not exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: מֵתוֹ וּמְשַׁמְּרוֹ — אִין, אֲבָל מְהַלֵּךְ בְּבֵית הַקְּבָרוֹת — לָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws an inference from the answer in step 11, setting up a new challenge
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Only a relative or a guard is exempt. Someone simply walking in a cemetery is not.

steps.title: A ברייתא forbids תפילין and reading תורה in a cemetery
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the inference with a ברייתא: one may not walk in a cemetery wearing תפילין or reading from a ספר תורה, because doing so is 'mocking the poor.'
steps.simpleTranslation: But wasn't it taught: A person should not walk in a cemetery with תפילין on his head and a ספר תורה in his arm while reading from it. If he does, he violates 'one who mocks the poor insults his Maker.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא showing that someone in a cemetery may NOT do certain מצוות, which seems to contradict step 12.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 12 said a person walking in a cemetery is not exempt, so he should be fully obligated. But the ברייתא says he must not wear תפילין or read the תורה there. That means he is effectively released from those מצוות, just like the relative and the guard.

keyTerms.meaning: Mocks the poor one. The dead are 'poor' because they can no longer do מצוות.

phrases.aramaic: וְהָתַנְיָא: לֹא יְהַלֵּךְ אָדָם בְּבֵית הַקְּבָרוֹת
phrases.english: But wasn't it taught: A person should not walk in a cemetery
with תפילין on his head
and a ספר תורה in his arm, while reading from it.
And if he does so,
he violates 'One who mocks the poor insults his Maker.'
phrases.notes: משלי 17:5

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָתַנְיָא: לֹא יְהַלֵּךְ אָדָם בְּבֵית הַקְּבָרוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the inference of step 12
steps.kashyaTarget: The inference that one walking in a cemetery is not exempt
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא forbids תפילין and reading תורה in a cemetery, so such a person is released from those מצוות

steps.title: Within four אמות versus beyond four אמות
steps.stepSummary: In a cemetery, the restriction applies only within ארבע אמות of a grave. Beyond that, he is obligated. A relative or a guard is exempt even beyond ארבע אמות.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, in the cemetery, it is forbidden only within four אמות of the grave; beyond four אמות he is obligated, as the master said: a מת takes up four אמות for קריאת שמע. Here, with a relative or a guard, he is exempt even beyond four אמות.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by marking the difference between the two cases: how far the rule reaches.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The cemetery rule is about not mocking the dead, so it only applies close to the grave, within the 'space' a מת takes up. The relative or guard is exempt because of his responsibility for the body, so his exemption applies no matter how far away he is. That is why step 12's distinction still works.
steps.whatToRemember: A relative or a guard of a מת is exempt from מצוות even at a distance. In a cemetery, the restriction applies only within ארבע אמות of a grave.
steps.whyThisMatters: This gives the practical rule of ארבע אמות around a grave for קריאת שמע, תפילין and learning תורה.

phrases.aramaic: הָתָם, תּוֹךְ אַרְבַּע אַמּוֹת הוּא דְאָסוּר,
phrases.english: There, it is within four cubits that it is forbidden,
but beyond four cubits, he is obligated.
As the master said:

phrases.aramaic: מֵת תּוֹפֵס אַרְבַּע אַמּוֹת לִקְרִיאַת שְׁמַע.
phrases.english: A dead body takes up four cubits regarding קריאת שמע.
phrases.notes: He means that within four cubits of a dead body you may not say שמע.

phrases.aramaic: הָכָא, חוּץ לְאַרְבַּע אַמּוֹת נָמֵי פָּטוּר.
phrases.english: Here, even beyond four cubits he is also exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָתָם, תּוֹךְ אַרְבַּע אַמּוֹת הוּא דְאָסוּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 13
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Walking in a cemetery creates the same exemption as being a relative or guard
steps.terutzMaskana: The cemetery rule applies only within four אמות. The relative or guard is exempt at any distance.

steps.title: Returning to the ברייתא about guarding the dead
steps.stepSummary: With 'גופא' the גמרא goes back to quote the guard ברייתא in full, so it can study the rest of it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Now to the ברייתא itself: One who guards a dead body, even if it is not his relative, is exempt from קריאת שמע, תפילה, תפילין, and all the מצוות of the תורה.
steps.whatsHappening: This is a setup line. The גמרא repeats the ברייתא from step 10 so it can now quote and learn the rest of it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before, the ברייתא was used only as a challenge. Now the גמרא goes back to it to learn its other details, about two guards and about a boat.

keyTerms.meaning: 'The matter itself': going back to study a source quoted earlier

phrases.english: Now to the matter itself:

phrases.aramaic: הַמְשַׁמֵּר אֶת הַמֵּת אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵינוֹ מֵתוֹ —
phrases.english: One who guards the dead, even though it is not his dead relative,
is exempt from קריאת שמע and from prayer,
and from תפילין,
and from all the מצוות stated in the תורה.

steps.triggerLanguage: גּוּפָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new section that studies the ברייתא from step 10
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A guard of the dead, even if not a relative, is exempt from all מצוות

steps.title: Two guards take turns
steps.stepSummary: If there are two guards, they take turns: one guards while the other reads, and then they switch.
steps.simpleTranslation: If there were two of them, this one guards while that one reads, and then that one guards while this one reads.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא continues: when two people are guarding, each one can do his מצוות while the other guards.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The guard is exempt only because he is busy guarding. If someone else can guard, he is no longer busy, so he must do the מצוות. The exemption depends on actually being needed.

keyTerms.meaning: This one guards and that one reads

phrases.english: If there were two,
this one guards and that one reads,
phrases.notes: 'Reads' means reads קריאת שמע.

phrases.english: and then that one guards and this one reads.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָיוּ שְׁנַיִם — זֶה מְשַׁמֵּר וְזֶה קוֹרֵא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ברייתא with a case of two guards
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Two guards take turns guarding and saying קריאת שמע

steps.title: בן עזאי: on a boat both may pray in another corner
steps.stepSummary: בן עזאי says that if they are traveling with the body on a boat, they put it in one corner and both pray in another corner.
steps.simpleTranslation: בן עזאי says: If they were traveling on a boat, they set the body down in this corner, and both of them pray in another corner.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא ends with בן עזאי's rule for a special case: traveling with a body on a boat.
steps.deeperAnalysis: On a boat, the body is safe from animals, so it does not need active guarding. That means both people can pray at the same time without taking turns. The exemption stops when real guarding is not needed.
steps.whatToRemember: The guard's exemption depends on guarding really being needed. With two guards they take turns, and on a boat (according to בן עזאי) both may pray.

phrases.english: בן עזאי says:
If they were traveling on a boat,
he sets it down in this corner,
and both of them pray in another corner.

steps.triggerLanguage: בֶּן עַזַּאי אוֹמֵר: הָיוּ בָּאִים בִּסְפִינָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another opinion about a special case, a boat
steps.mimraCoreRuling: On a boat, the body may be left in one corner while both pray in another corner

steps.title: What is the difference between the two views?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what practical difference there is between the first view (the guards take turns) and בן עזאי (on a boat, both may pray in a corner).
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the difference between them?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks how the first view and בן עזאי actually differ in practice. This sets up רבינא's answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first view requires someone to guard the body at all times, even while the other guard prays. בן עזאי allows both to pray on a boat with the body left in a corner. The גמרא wants the exact reason behind this disagreement.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the difference between them? (asks for the practical result of a disagreement)

phrases.english: What is the difference between them?
phrases.notes: "Them" means the first view (guards take turns, Step 16) and בן עזאי (the boat, Step 17).

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי בֵּינַיְיהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks what separates בן עזאי's boat ruling from the first view.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The practical point on which the first view and בן עזאי disagree.

steps.title: The difference is whether we worry about mice
steps.stepSummary: רבינא answers that they disagree about whether we worry that mice may harm the body, even on a boat.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said: The difference between them is whether we are worried about mice. One view holds we are worried; the other holds we are not.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא explains that the disagreement is about mice. The first view worries that mice could reach the body even on a boat, so someone must always guard it. בן עזאי does not worry about this on a boat.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Everyone agrees that a guard's job is to protect the body from harm. The only question is whether mice are a real danger on a boat. If they are, someone must always guard. If not, both people may pray at the same time.

keyTerms.meaning: We are worried about / we take into account
One master holds... and the other master holds (lays out two sides)

steps.whatToRemember: The guards ברייתא and בן עזאי differ only about whether mice are a danger on a boat.

phrases.english: Ravina said:
Whether we are worried about mice is the difference between them.
One master holds: we are worried.
phrases.notes: This is the first view, which requires one guard to stay with the body at all times.

phrases.english: And the other master holds: we are not worried.
phrases.notes: This is בן עזאי, who allows both to pray on the boat.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבִינָא: חוֹשְׁשִׁין לְעַכְבָּרִים אִיכָּא בֵּינַיְיהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 18.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: They disagree about whether mice are a danger to the body even on a boat.

steps.title: Do not ride on a bag of bones, unless you are in danger
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that someone carrying bones may not put them in a saddlebag and sit on them, because that is disrespectful. If he fears non-Jews or robbers, it is allowed. The same applies to a ספר תורה.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: Someone carrying bones from place to place may not put them in a saddlebag, put it on a donkey, and ride on them, because he treats them with disrespect. But if he is afraid of non-Jews or robbers, it is allowed. And just as they said about bones, so they said about a ספר תורה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא about respecting a dead person's bones while moving them. It has a rule (no riding on them), an exception (danger), and a comparison to a ספר תורה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Sitting on something treats it like ordinary luggage, which shames the dead. When there is danger, he needs to move fast and safely, so the rule gives way. The last line about a ספר תורה is unclear: which part of the ברייתא does it compare to? The next step asks exactly that.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
One who carries bones from place to place,
he may not put them in a saddlebag
and put them on a donkey's back
and ride on them,
because he treats them with disrespect.
But if he was afraid of non-Jews
or of robbers, it is allowed.
And just as they said about bones,
so they said about a Torah scroll.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: הַמּוֹלִיךְ עֲצָמוֹת מִמָּקוֹם לְמָקוֹם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to a new ברייתא on the same general theme of respecting the dead.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One may not ride on bones carried in a saddlebag, since it is disrespectful, but in danger it is allowed. The same applies to a ספר תורה.

steps.title: Which part does the ספר תורה line refer to?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks which clause the ספר תורה comparison refers to. It cannot be the first clause, because that would be obvious: a ספר תורה is surely no less important than bones.
steps.simpleTranslation: To which part does this refer? If you say it refers to the first part, that is obvious! Is a ספר תורה any less important than bones?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks which part of the ברייתא the ספר תורה line refers to. It rules out the first part, which sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the line only meant that you may not ride on a ספר תורה, it would teach nothing new. Of course a ספר תורה deserves at least as much respect as bones. So the line must be teaching something less obvious.

keyTerms.meaning: To which one? (which clause is meant)
The first part of a teaching
Is it any worse / less important?

phrases.english: To which part does this refer?
If you say it refers to the first part, that is obvious!
phrases.notes: The first part is the ban on riding on the bones.

phrases.english: Is a Torah scroll any less important than bones?

steps.triggerLanguage: אַהֵיָיא? אִילֵּימָא אַרֵישָׁא — פְּשִׁיטָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about the unclear final line of the ברייתא in Step 20.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the ספר תורה comparison refers to the ban or to the danger exception.

steps.title: It refers to the danger exception
steps.stepSummary: The ספר תורה line refers to the last clause: in danger, one may even ride on a ספר תורה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it refers to the last part.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא concludes that the comparison is to the danger exception. Even a ספר תורה may be carried this way when a person fears non-Jews or robbers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The new lesson is not that a ספר תורה deserves respect, which we already knew. The lesson is that even something as holy as a ספר תורה may be put in a saddlebag and ridden on when there is real danger.

keyTerms.meaning: The last part of a teaching

steps.confusionAlert: Do not read this as making a ספר תורה less holy. The ban on riding on it stays in place; only the danger exception now applies to it too.
steps.whatToRemember: In real danger, one may even ride on a ספר תורה in a saddlebag, just like bones.

phrases.english: Rather, it refers to the last part.
phrases.notes: The last part is the exception: if he's afraid of non-Jews or robbers, it's allowed.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אַסֵּיפָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 21.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The ספר תורה comparison refers to the danger exception: in danger, it is allowed.

steps.title: Not escorting a מת is mocking the poor
steps.stepSummary: רחבה, quoting רב יהודה, teaches that anyone who sees a מת being taken to burial and does not escort him violates the idea of 'mocking the poor.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רחבה said in the name of רב יהודה: Anyone who sees a מת and does not escort him transgresses 'Whoever mocks the poor insults his Maker.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new teaching about honoring the dead. Ignoring a funeral you see passing is treated as mocking the poor.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The dead person is the 'poor one,' since he can no longer do anything for himself. Walking past without joining shows contempt for his helpless state. This matches the 'mocking the poor' idea from earlier in the סוגיא.
steps.whyThisMatters: This teaching is a source for the practice of joining a funeral procession you come across.

phrases.english: Rachava said that Rav Yehuda said:
Anyone who sees a dead person and does not escort him
transgresses because of "Whoever mocks the poor insults his Maker."
phrases.notes: משלי 17:5

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַחֲבָה אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה: כָּל הָרוֹאֶה הַמֵּת וְאֵינוֹ מְלַוֵּהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new teaching on honoring the dead.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Seeing a מת and not escorting him counts as mocking the poor.

steps.title: What is the reward for escorting?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what reward a person gets if he does escort the מת.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if he does escort him, what is his reward?
steps.whatsHappening: Having taught the penalty for not escorting, the גמרא now asks about the reward for escorting. This sets up רב אסי's answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question turns the teaching around, from what you lose by ignoring a funeral to what you gain by joining one.

phrases.english: And if he did escort him, what is his reward?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִם הִלְוָהוּ מַה שְּׂכָרוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows up on Step 23 with the positive side.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The reward for escorting a מת.

steps.title: Escorting the dead is a loan to ה׳ and honors Him
steps.stepSummary: רב אסי answers with פסוקים: escorting the מת is like lending to ה׳, who repays, and showing grace to the poor honors ה׳.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אסי said: About him the פסוק says, 'One who is gracious to the poor lends to ה׳,' and 'One who is gracious to the needy honors Him.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב אסי answers that the reward is great: the person is treated as lending to ה׳ and honoring Him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word מלוה can mean both 'escorts' and 'lends,' so the פסוק is read as being about escorting the dead. The מת is the poor one who cannot repay, so ה׳ Himself repays. Being kind to the helpless is a way of honoring their Creator.

keyTerms.meaning: Lends to ה׳ (here also read as 'escorting')

steps.whatToRemember: Not escorting a מת mocks the poor and insults ה׳. Escorting him is like lending to ה׳ and honoring Him.

phrases.english: Rav Asi said:
About him the verse says:
"One who is gracious to the poor lends to the Lord"
phrases.notes: משלי 19:17. מלוה can also sound like 'escorts', which is why this פסוק fits here.

phrases.english: and "One who is gracious to the needy honors Him."
phrases.notes: משלי 14:31

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב אַסִּי, עָלָיו הַכָּתוּב אוֹמֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 24.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: One who escorts the dead is considered to lend to ה׳, who repays him, and to honor ה׳.

steps.title: רבי חייא tells רבי יונתן to lift his ציצית in the cemetery
steps.stepSummary: While walking in a cemetery, רבי יונתן's תכלת string drags on the ground. רבי חייא tells him to lift it so the dead will not feel insulted.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חייא and רבי יונתן were walking in a cemetery, and the תכלת string of רבי יונתן's ציצית was dragging on the ground. רבי חייא said to him: Lift it up, so the dead won't say, 'Tomorrow they'll be buried here with us, and now they insult us.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a story that connects to the theme of respecting the dead. רבי חייא tells his friend to pick up his dragging ציצית string in the cemetery.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי חייא assumes the dead are aware of what the living do around them. He holds that a visible display of a מצוה among the graves could hurt their feelings. This assumption is what the next step will challenge.

keyTerms.meaning: the sky-blue (תכלת) string of the ציצית

phrases.english: Rabbi Chiya and Rabbi Yonatan
were walking in a cemetery.
The sky-blue string of Rabbi Yonatan's tzitzis was dragging on the ground.
Rabbi Chiya said to him: Lift it up,
so that they will not say:
phrases.notes: 'They' means the dead buried in this cemetery.

phrases.english: Tomorrow they are coming to join us,
and now they are insulting us.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי חִיָּיא וְרַבִּי יוֹנָתָן הֲווֹ שָׁקְלִי וְאָזְלִי בְּבֵית הַקְּבָרוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the theme of honoring the dead through a story. It applies the step 13 rule against displaying מצוות in a בית הקברות in a way that mocks the dead.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One should not display a מצוה (such as hanging ציצית) in a cemetery in a way that would shame the dead.

steps.title: רבי יונתן asks: do the dead really know anything?
steps.stepSummary: רבי יונתן challenges רבי חייא's assumption, quoting a פסוק that says the dead know nothing.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יונתן said to him: Do the dead know so much? Isn't it written, 'And the dead know nothing'?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יונתן pushes back on רבי חייא. He quotes a פסוק to show that the dead are not aware of what we do.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge targets the hidden assumption behind רבי חייא's instruction, that the dead can notice and feel insulted. If the פסוק in קהלת means the dead are completely unaware, there is no reason to lift the ציצית.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: וּמִי יָדְעִי כּוּלֵּי הַאי?
phrases.english: He said to him: Do they know so much?
But isn't it written:
"And the dead know nothing"!
phrases.notes: קהלת 9:5

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמִי יָדְעִי כּוּלֵּי הַאי? וְהָא כְּתִיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the assumption behind רבי חייא's instruction.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי חייא's assumption that the dead are aware and can feel insulted.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A פסוק explicitly says the dead know nothing, so they cannot be insulted by the ציצית.

steps.title: רבי חייא says the פסוק was not studied deeply enough
steps.stepSummary: רבי חייא gently scolds רבי יונתן for not reviewing and understanding the פסוק properly. This sets up his new reading.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: If you read the פסוק, you didn't read it a second time. If you read it twice, you didn't read it a third time. If you read it three times, nobody explained it to you properly.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי חייא begins his answer by saying the פסוק has been misunderstood. He is setting up his correct explanation, which comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He does not deny the פסוק. He claims its plain surface meaning is not its real meaning. The line also teaches that real understanding takes repeated review and a teacher's explanation.

keyTerms.meaning: you repeated it a second time
you went over it a third time

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אִם קָרִיתָ — לֹא שָׁנִיתָ.
phrases.english: He said to him: If you read it, you did not read it a second time.
If you read it a second time, you did not read it a third time.
If you read it a third time, they did not explain it to you.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִם קָרִיתָ — לֹא שָׁנִיתָ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens רבי חייא's defense against רבי יונתן's challenge.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The פסוק means simply that all dead people are unaware.
steps.terutzMaskana: The פסוק has a deeper meaning that רבי יונתן missed, explained next.

steps.title: The 'living' in the פסוק are the צדיקים, even after death
steps.stepSummary: רבי חייא rereads the first half of the same פסוק. 'The living' refers to צדיקים, who are called living even when they have died.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'For the living know that they will die': these are the צדיקים, who even in their death are called living.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי חייא starts explaining the פסוק correctly, beginning with its first half. 'The living' there does not just mean people who are alive. It means the righteous.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By redefining 'the living' as צדיקים, he opens the door to saying that the dead צדיקים do know things. So the word 'dead' in the פסוק cannot mean every person in the grave.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't think רבי חייא ignores the פסוק's words 'the dead know nothing.' He is rereading the whole פסוק, and here he explains its first half, about 'the living.'

phrases.english: "For the living know that they will die"
phrases.notes: This is the opening of the same פסוק רבי יונתן quoted, קהלת 9:5.

phrases.english: these are the righteous
who even in their death are called living,

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי הַחַיִּים יוֹדְעִים שֶׁיָּמוּתוּ — אֵלּוּ צַדִּיקִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Delivers the explanation promised in the scolding of the previous step.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'The living' means people physically alive, and 'the dead' means everyone in the grave.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'The living' are the צדיקים, who are considered alive even after death.

steps.title: Proof from the פסוק about בניהו בן יהוידע
steps.stepSummary: רבי חייא cites a פסוק describing בניהו בן יהוידע as the son of a 'living man.' This is meant to prove that צדיקים are called living.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is said: 'And בניהו son of יהוידע, son of a living man, of many deeds, from קבצאל. He struck the two altar-hearths of מואב, and he went down and struck the lion inside the pit on a snowy day.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי חייא brings a פסוק to support his claim that צדיקים are called 'living.' He quotes it here, and the גמרא explains how it proves the point right after this.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof rests on the phrase 'son of a living man' (בן איש חי). It seems odd to describe a father this way, which hints at a deeper meaning. That explanation is spelled out in the next lines of the גמרא.

keyTerms.meaning: בניהו son of יהוידע, דוד's great warrior

phrases.english: as it is said:
"And Benayahu son of Yehoyada,

phrases.aramaic: בֶּן אִישׁ חַי רַב פְּעָלִים מִקַּבְצְאֵל
phrases.english: son of a living man, of many deeds, from Kabze'el,
phrases.notes: שמואל ב 23:20. The word to watch is חי, 'living'; the גמרא explains it right after this.

phrases.aramaic: הוּא הִכָּה אֵת שְׁנֵי אֲרִאֵל מוֹאָב
phrases.english: he struck the two altar-hearths of Moab;
and he went down and struck the lion
inside the pit on a day of snow."

steps.triggerLanguage: שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: וּבְנָיָהוּ בֶן יְהוֹיָדָע בֶּן אִישׁ חַי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies a scriptural source for the claim that צדיקים are called living after death.
steps.raayaObject: The claim that צדיקים are called 'living' even in death.
steps.raayaSupportSource: שמואל ב 23:20, which calls בניהו 'son of a living man' (בן איש חי).
